title: Ideal gases
summary: The ideal gas model relates pressure, volume, temperature and amount. Know its assumptions, why real gases deviate, and use the gas laws and pV = nRT.

keyterms.definition: A model gas whose particles have negligible volume, no intermolecular forces and perfectly elastic collisions.
An actual gas; it deviates from ideal behaviour most at high pressure and low temperature.
Force per unit area, caused by gas particles colliding with the container walls; SI unit Pa.
Volume occupied by one mole of gas; 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ at STP (273.15 K, 100 kPa) for an ideal gas.
Standard temperature and pressure: 273.15 K and 100 kPa.
pV = nRT, with p in Pa, V in m³, T in K and R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
At constant temperature and amount, pressure is inversely proportional to volume (pV = constant).
At constant pressure and amount, volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature.
At constant volume and amount, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.
p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂ for a fixed amount of gas.

questions.prompt: Which is an assumption of the ideal gas model?
questions.explanation: Ideal gas particles are treated as points with no forces between them and elastic collisions.

questions.statement: Real gases behave most ideally at high temperature and low pressure.
questions.explanation: Particles are far apart (volume negligible) and move fast enough that attractions matter little.

questions.prompt: Why does a real gas deviate from ideal behaviour at very high pressure?
options: Particle volume becomes significant compared with the container volume
questions.explanation: When squeezed, the particles themselves take up a significant fraction of the space.

questions.text: At low temperature, real gases deviate because intermolecular ___ become significant.
questions.explanation: Slow particles are pulled together by intermolecular forces, lowering the pressure below the ideal value.

questions.prompt: Match each gas law to the variables held constant.
questions.explanation: Each law links two variables while the other two are fixed.

questions.statement: Gas pressure is caused by particles colliding with the walls of the container.
questions.explanation: Each collision exerts a force; the total force per unit area is the pressure.

questions.prompt: Which gas is likely to deviate most from ideal behaviour under the same conditions?
questions.explanation: NH₃ molecules are polar and hydrogen bond, so intermolecular attractions are strongest.

questions.text: The molar volume of an ideal gas at STP is ___ dm³ mol⁻¹.
questions.explanation: At 273.15 K and 100 kPa (the IB STP) the molar volume is 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹.

questions.prompt: Order these conditions from most ideal to least ideal behaviour for nitrogen.
questions.explanation: Ideal behaviour improves with higher temperature and lower pressure.

questions.prompt: What is the volume of 0.500 mol of an ideal gas at STP?
A gas occupies 2.0 dm³ at 100 kPa. At constant temperature, its volume at 400 kPa is…
questions.explanation: Boyle's law: p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ → V₂ = 100 × 2.0 / 400 = 0.50 dm³.

questions.text: In pV = nRT, the temperature must be in ___.
questions.explanation: Gas laws use absolute temperature, which is zero when particle motion is minimal.

questions.statement: Doubling the Celsius temperature of a gas at constant pressure doubles its volume.
questions.explanation: Volume is proportional to absolute (kelvin) temperature: going from 20 °C to 40 °C is 293 K to 313 K, only about a 7 % increase.

questions.prompt: How many moles of gas are in 0.0240 m³ at 100 kPa and 300 K? (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)

questions.text: A volume of 500 cm³ in SI units is ___ m³.
questions.explanation: 1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³, so 500 cm³ = 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³.

questions.prompt: Match each graph (fixed amount of ideal gas) to its shape.

pairs.left: V against T in K (constant p)

questions.explanation: pV is constant at constant T, so a pV–p plot is flat.

questions.prompt: A sealed rigid can of gas is heated from 300 K to 450 K. The pressure…
questions.explanation: Gay-Lussac: p ∝ T at constant V, so p increases by 450/300 = 1.5.

questions.statement: The molar mass of a gas can be found from its mass, p, V and T using pV = (m/M)RT.
questions.explanation: Rearranging gives M = mRT/(pV).

questions.prompt: Order the steps to find the molar mass of a volatile liquid by vaporizing it in a gas syringe.
items: Inject and vaporize it at a known temperature
Read the gas volume and pressure
questions.explanation: This is a common practical use of the ideal gas equation.

questions.prompt: A gas at 200 kPa, 1.00 dm³ and 250 K is changed to 100 kPa and 500 K. What is its new volume?
